extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters (or screenwriters-turned-novelists) adapting a screenplay into a novel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for screenwriters who want to convert a screenplay into a published prose work, explaining the major craft and structural differences and the practical steps to expand a script into a novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose sensibility vs. screenplay sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Screenwriters and novelists respond to complexity very differently. Screenplay mantra: "Keep it clear; Less is more; Show, don’t tell; Get to the emotional point, and move on; Move fast and don’t waste time with exposition beyond what you need to set the scene." Novel mantra: "Show, don’t tell, but exposition is your friend, and a necessary one; You have no strict length constraints, so write, write, write; Go deep, go long; leave no emotional stone unturned."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key obligation: develop a prose voice and prose sensibility — this is a new craft that must be learned. 'Story real estate' is far larger for novels (no strict page/time limits), so you must learn to fill that space with depth, emotional resonance, backstory, and language rather than the extreme economy of scripts. Practical advice: invest in good teachers, get critiques from voracious book readers (not screenwriters), expect to do lots of prose practice and rewrites. Anti-patterns: treating the screenplay as the sole guide, relying on screenwriter-style brevity in exposition, or expecting a screenplay sensibility to suffice for prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view, voice, & tense
rubrics_metrics.description: POV, narrative voice, and tense are complex and central in novels; screenplays are typically third person, present tense and convey voice largely through dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelists can choose between multiple POVs (first-person, omniscient, third-person limited, third-person unlimited, second-person) and past or present tense; these choices profoundly affect narrative intimacy and information control. Screenwriters must experiment with POV and tense in prose (and be prepared to rewrite entire books changing these choices). The page's toolkit lists common POVs and their effects (omniscient observer voice; first-person 'I' limited knowledge; third-person limited through one character; third-person unlimited shifting viewpoints; second-person addressed 'you').

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplots and supporting characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Screenplays often have one or two subplots; novels typically require multiple subplots to support a longer middle and to expand supporting characters into their own 'stories within the story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To expand a screenplay into a three- or four-hundred page novel you will likely need two, three, or four sub-stories. Look to key supporting characters and create their own arcs to enrich the main narrative and sustain the middle. Types of subplots to consider include need subplots, expositional/background subplots, and thematic subplots. Anti-pattern: failing to create sufficient subplotting, which leaves the middle thin and causes pacing collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative scope and choosing the right prose container
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand prose 'containers' and their word-count/structural expectations before adapting: short story (≤7,500), novelette (7,500–17,000), novella (17,000–30,000), novel (30,000+).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screenwriters must study prose forms to determine which container fits their story and how the required scope changes structural choices and pacing. Each prose format has its own 'oddities and demands' that influence how much to expand plotlines, characters, and exposition. Misjudging scope can lead to under- or over-stretched narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reworking the premise (don't treat the script as only an outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: The screenplay's premise will almost always have to be reinvented to build in subplots, new action lines, and more complex story elements; using the script as a simple outline usually fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a mindset that you will likely retool the story from the ground up rather than merely expanding beats. Expect to change premise elements, restructure story priorities, and add material that wasn't in the script. Anti-pattern: following script beats slavishly with the expectation that that will produce a successful novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition: balancing showing and telling in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Screenplays require showing almost exclusively; novels allow and often require more telling (exposition). Screenwriters often err in two opposite ways: producing rambling, overly detailed descriptions or producing stunted, fragmentary exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn to leverage additional story real estate to deepen character motivations and worldbuilding using lyrical, organic exposition rather than verbosity or purple prose. Watch for two main potholes: rambling/purple prose that breaks narrative flow and short, curt exposition that fails to fill necessary gaps. The solution is balance: use economy of words with meaningful content and proper pacing; fill expositional holes organically rather than padding for length.
